source.title: Med-SegLens: Latent-Level Model Diffing for Interpretable Medical Image Segmentation
source.authors: Salma J. Ahmed; Emad A. Mohammed; Azam Asilian Bidgoli

record.tranche_reason: The paper directly sweeps SAE dictionary expansion factors and reports how feature specificity and splitting change, using the same general size-scaling question in medical segmentation models.
record.gate_note: Appendix B.2 reports the dictionary-size sweep. Other SAE results in the paper concern cross-dataset alignment, interventions, or latent semantics rather than splitting as dictionary size changes. The paper does not match individual features across sizes or measure whether their inputs partition or their directions remain close.
record.test_reason: The dictionary-size sweep (Appendix B.2) is a hyperparameter ablation used to pick expansion factor 16. Figure 11 reports only reconstruction error, explained variance and dead-feature fraction. The statement that larger expansions 'encourage feature splitting' is asserted, citing Bricken et al., with no splitting measure. No feature is tracked across sizes, and input coverage and decoder-direction proximity are never measured. The paper's own results concern cross-dataset latent alignment and steering, not splitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record overstates the splitting result. The authors' main conclusion is that cross-dataset latent diffing separates shared from population-specific latents, and that steering the latter recovers segmentation failures without retraining. On dictionary size, they only state, citing Bricken et al., that larger expansions encourage splitting but raise dead features, and choose factor 16 as the best trade-off. They do not measure splitting.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses BatchTopK SAEs on segmentation-model activations and compares expansion factors 8, 16, and 32; it does not perform feature-by-feature matching across dictionary sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: Expansion factor changes feature breadth, splitting, and dead-feature fraction; the authors select 16 as the best trade-off.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed expansion factor of 16, multiple SAE latents emerge per tumor or anatomical class, varying by location, morphology, scale and depth (Section 4.1, Appendix D, Figure 13). The evidence is qualitative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAEs on vision segmentation models assign several fine-grained latents to a single semantic class at a fixed dictionary size.

fits_no_version.finding: The dead-feature fraction rises with expansion factor (8→16→32) for BatchTopK SAEs on SegFormer activations (Figure 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger SAE dictionaries yield more dead latents in vision segmentation SAEs.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: For the dictionary-size claim, the reported results are qualitative; no numerical feature-level comparisons, input-partition measures, or directional similarities are supplied. The study reports a higher dead-feature fraction and excessive fragmentation at larger expansion.

untested.parts: All parts. No coarse feature is traced to finer features at larger sizes, and input coverage and direction proximity are not measured.
All parts. Multiple latents per tumor class are shown qualitatively, but no hierarchy or geometric family analysis is done.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T1' and its supports label for V1 are not justified: no row measures splitting. Figure 11 values themselves are not given numerically in the text.

versions.untested_parts: It does not track an individual coarse feature into several larger-dictionary features, measure whether those features cover roughly the same inputs, or measure proximity of their directions.

rows.subject: SegFormer trained on the adult dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE expansion factors of 8, 16, and 32.
rows.measure: Feature breadth and specificity as dictionary size varies
rows.value: Smaller expansion factors produce broader, less interpretable features; expansion factor 8 is described as underfitting.
rows.note: This is consistent with smaller dictionaries yielding broader features, but the paper does not identify a particular coarse feature or measure its inputs or direction.
rows.check: Qualitative description of size-8 features as 'broader, less specific' with no measure of breadth or specificity. Figure 11 shows only reconstruction and dead-feature metrics, so it cannot show V1's effect.

rows.subject: SegFormer trained on the adult dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE expansion factors of 8, 16, and 32.
rows.measure: Reconstruction fidelity, active feature use, and semantic interpretability
rows.value: Expansion factor 16 is reported to provide the best balance across these criteria.
rows.note: The reported balance does not establish whether coarse features split into input-covering, nearby-direction features.
rows.check: Selection value: the choice of expansion factor 16 as best trade-off is a hyperparameter choice, not a result on splitting. It should not be a row.

rows.subject: SegFormer trained on the adult dataset
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE expansion factors of 8, 16, and 32.
rows.value: Larger expansions encourage feature splitting, but have a substantially higher fraction of dead features and are described as causing excessive feature fragmentation.
rows.note: The text reports a splitting tendency but gives no individual feature correspondences, input coverage, or directional-distance result.
rows.check: 'Encourage feature splitting' is an assertion supported by a citation (Bricken et al., 2023) rather than by any reported splitting measure. Only the dead-feature fraction is actually measured; that fraction is a different construct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SegFormer adult-dataset SAE expansion sweep, especially expansion factor 32
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that larger expansions encourage feature splitting, consistent with the size-related splitting tendency in V1; this does not establish input partitioning or nearby directions (r1, r3).
